Where the readout actually lands, drawn on a real frame instead of a stand-in

The approved mockup's own footer says its placement is not yet honest: it was drawn against a stand-in background, so “where it docks, what it overlaps and how it survives at low resolution all need a live frame before implementation.” This page is that check, on a real 2560×1440 frame of a live match. Every rectangle below is at its true screen pixel position, computed from the same constants the widget uses — the frame is scaled for viewing, the geometry is not.

The corner it docks in, and why it is the only one left · frame shown at 55%

chat root — 550 wide, centred, bottom-anchored
TRANSIENTS_PANEL — X:5, Y: WINDOW_HEIGHT-135, 550×80
DEFCON readout — X:5, W:352, bottom edge 1300
DEFCON 1OPEN WAR —
Everything is released. Units engage on sight.
NUCLEAR RELEASERELEASE IN 7:12
HOLD1kt20kt 50kt100kt200kt+
No warhead may be fired yet. Both sides are released at the same moment.

Four things already own a corner, and between them they leave exactly one. The right 250 px is the sidebar for the full height of the window. The bottom centre is the chat root. The bottom left is TRANSIENTS_PANEL, whose top edge is y 1305 — the readout's bottom edge is 1300, five pixels clear of it. And the left edge above the readout is the support-power column, which at sixteen icons of 62×46 can reach y 750, so the readout must not grow upward past roughly y 1100. It does not: 170 px of reserve, 162 px used at the tallest state.

The three states, at 1:1 · this is the real pixel size on a 2560×1440 screen

DEFCON 2WEAPONS FREE —
Your units will not fire on their own. Every shot is one you order.

DEFCON 1 — the nuclear block stacks above

DEFCON 1OPEN WAR —
Everything is released. Units engage on sight.
NUCLEAR RELEASE20 kt
HOLD1kt20kt 50kt100kt200kt+
Both sides are released to the same yield. Each use raises it.

The rule line wraps at DEFCON 2 and the strip grows upward, because both blocks are bottom-anchored to a fixed edge. That is what keeps the strip in one place for a whole match: a top-anchored layout would slide it down the screen the moment the nuclear block appeared, and the player would lose the position they had learned. DEFCON 1 is the only level where both blocks are on screen at once, and it is also the shortest strip — which is why 170 px of reserve is enough.

The transition banner · full width, four seconds, then gone

DEFCON 1
A life has been taken. Autonomous fire is released.
y 448, height 96 — (WINDOW_HEIGHT - HEIGHT) / 3

It runs off both edges of the screen deliberately, so it reads as the screen changing state rather than as a dialog asking for something. A third of the way down clears the top-centre notification area and sits well above the chat.

What this page is not. The geometry is real and the copy is the shipped strings, but the type is the browser's, not the engine's — the widget draws FreeSans through SpriteFont at sizes 10/12/14/24, and this page approximates that with whatever grotesque your system has. So line breaks, the exact width of the wrapped rule line and the vertical centring inside the step boxes are all indicative here and authoritative only in a real frame. Judge placement, overlap and whether 352 px is enough from this; judge legibility and wrapping from the capture.
